scenario.context: ShopSwift's app checkout conversion fell from 22% to 17% last week. Traffic is stable. A new app version shipped on Tuesday.

steps.task: List your hypotheses, what data you would pull for each, and name the most likely root cause.
hints: Slice the drop by platform, version, step and payment method.
Match the timing to the release.

hypotheses.check: Conversion by app version and OS
Funnel by step and payment method
Fee shown at checkout, by cohort

content.finding: The drop is only on Android v4.2 and only at the payment step for UPI. Root cause: a broken UPI intent call in v4.2. Action: roll back or hotfix and monitor payment success rate.

reference.whyItWorks: Segment first, then drill, and tie the timing to a change.
commonMistakes: No data plan for each hypothesis

scenario.context: MeetMint is a video-meeting app. D30 retention for October sign-ups is 33%, down from 41%. Two things changed: paid social went from 15% to 45% of sign-ups, and the free-plan meeting limit fell from 60 to 40 minutes. D30 retention for paid-social users is 25% in both periods. For all other channels it fell from 44% to 40%.

steps.task: Work out how much of the 8-point drop each change explains and state the root cause.
hints: Separate the mix effect from the within-channel effect.
Hold one factor constant and recompute.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Mix effect: the share of low-retention paid-social sign-ups rose from 15% to 45%
hypotheses.check: Keep other-channel retention at 44% with the new mix: 0.45 × 25 + 0.55 × 44 ≈ 35.5, so mix explains about 5.7 points

hypotheses.hypothesis: Limit effect: the free-plan meeting limit fell from 60 to 40 minutes, lowering retention in other channels
hypotheses.check: Other-channel retention fell from 44% to 40%, weighted at 55%, so the limit explains about 2.2 points

content.finding: Before: 0.15 × 25 + 0.85 × 44 ≈ 41. After: 0.45 × 25 + 0.55 × 40 ≈ 33. Root cause: mostly a shift toward low-retention paid-social users (about 70% of the drop), plus a smaller effect from the tighter free limit. Next steps: improve paid-social onboarding or targeting; A/B test the limit.

reference.whyItWorks: Decomposes the change into mix and rate instead of blaming one factor.

scenario.context: RunnerGo is a delivery-partner platform. In one city, active riders fell 12% in a month although applications rose 20%. Data: document verification time rose from 2 to 6 days; earnings per hour for riders with 3+ months' tenure fell 9% after an incentive cut; a competitor launched in the city two weeks ago.

steps.task: Build a cause tree for the fall in active riders, say what each data point implies, and state the root cause(s) and how you would confirm them.
hints: Active riders = new activations + retained riders.

hypotheses.check: Applications up 20% but verification takes 6 days, so many applicants drop before activation → check application-to-activation rate by wait time

hypotheses.hypothesis: Retention: incentive cut lowered earnings for tenured riders
hypotheses.check: Earnings per hour for riders with 3+ months' tenure fell 9% → check churn by tenure and by earnings change

hypotheses.hypothesis: Retention: competitor launch may add churn

content.finding: Root causes: (1) verification backlog cutting activations — supply is not lost at the top of the funnel, it is lost in the middle; (2) incentive cut raising churn among tenured riders; competitor effect likely secondary and recent. Confirm: cohort activation rate by verification time; churn before and after the incentive change; exit survey. Fix: add verification capacity, restore targeted incentives for tenured riders.

reference.whyItWorks: Splits the problem into funnel and retention and matches each fact to a branch.
commonMistakes: Blaming the competitor because it is visible
rubric: Competitor treated as secondary with reasoning
